title: A Bridge for the Letter
premise: In 1747, Wren Eastwick completes the coastal atlas his master died protecting, only to discover the master's handwriting arriving on letters from a man officially drowned three years past. The letters point to a hidden berth aboard a smuggling brig — one berth, and a family fractured by which of them deserves to flee the magistrate closing in. As Wren traces the atlas's coded margins toward the truth of his master's death, he learns survival was purchased with another man's name, and that the corpse writing letters is the price still owed. In the end Wren gives up the berth himself, sends his sister away with the finished atlas as her passport, and burns the master's confession so the living can stop paying for the dead.
about_author: Emrys Sandoval is a former cartographic archivist who spent a decade cataloguing smugglers' charts in coastal county records offices before turning to fiction. He writes historical novels about the documents people leave behind and the debts they encode.

chapters.title: The Last Plate
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. He inks the final plate of the dead master's atlas in a rain-stained workshop, rehearsing the silences that have kept him safe for three years. When a letter arrives bearing the master's unmistakable hand — signed by a drowned man — the careful order of his grief cracks open. Beat: dread disguised as routine.

chapters.title: A Stranger at the Door
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. The stranger, Callum Voss, claims the letters come from Tobias Marsh, the master supposedly lost at sea, and demands Wren decode the atlas's marginal cipher. Wren lies badly and Voss knows it. The workshop feels watched by nightfall. Beat: the first fissure in a constructed safety.

chapters.title: What the Margins Keep
chapters.summary: Wren's POV, with a flashback to his apprenticeship. He begins translating the margin notes and finds they are not navigational but confessional — payments made, names erased. His sister Bette notices his sleeplessness and presses him; he deflects, deepening the distance between them. Beat: knowledge as burden.

chapters.title: The Magistrate's Courtesy
chapters.summary: Magistrate Halloway's POV. Halloway pays a courteous visit to the workshop, admiring the nearly finished atlas while making clear he suspects it contains more than coastlines. He mentions Marsh's drowning with too much precision. Wren understands the atlas is evidence in someone's trial yet to come. Beat: polite menace.

chapters.title: Bette's Arithmetic
chapters.summary: Bette's POV. Bette, who has kept the household solvent since their father's ruin, calculates what flight would cost and concludes there is money for one passage, not two. She begins quietly selling their mother's silver without telling Wren. Beat: love expressed as secret accounting.

chapters.title: The Drowned Man's Hand
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. A second letter arrives, this one naming a date and a berth aboard the brig Kestrel. Wren compares the hand against the master's surviving drafts and confronts an unbearable possibility: either Marsh lives, or someone learned to write as him. Beat: grief destabilized into suspicion.

chapters.title: Voss's Bargain
chapters.summary: Voss's POV. Voss reveals he served under Marsh and believes the master faked his death to escape Halloway's corruption inquiry, leaving Voss to take the fall. He offers Wren a place on the Kestrel in exchange for the decoded margins. Wren refuses; Voss leaves a warning instead. Beat: coercion wearing friendship's face.

chapters.title: The Atlas Is Summoned
chapters.summary: Halloway's POV. Halloway formally requisitions the unfinished atlas for the Admiralty, giving Wren ten days. Privately he tells his clerk that whoever holds the margins holds proof against half the customs house. Wren realizes delivering the atlas protects no one. Beat: the trap closes politely.

chapters.title: Night Work
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Racing to finish and secretly copy the margins before surrendering the atlas, Wren works by candlelight while Bette stands watch. They argue about who leaves if escape becomes necessary — each insists the other goes. It is their first honest fight in years. Beat: devotion sharpened into conflict.

chapters.title: The Smuggler's Chapel
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Following a margin cipher to a ruined chapel, Wren meets a smuggler named Idris Fen who confirms Marsh is alive, hiding, and dying slowly of a wound taken the night of his 'drowning.' Fen delivers a third letter: Marsh wants Wren to bring the atlas itself. Beat: the dead man acquires a heartbeat.

chapters.title: What Master Wanted
chapters.summary: Flashback chapter, Marsh's POV, the night of the supposed drowning. Marsh staged his death to protect the atlas and its witnesses, paying a boatman with a lie that cost the boatman everything. He has watched Wren from a distance for three years, telling himself silence was protection. Beat: the mentor's love revealed as another kind of control.

chapters.title: The Berth
chapters.summary: Bette's POV. Bette learns the Kestrel sails in nine days with one berth paid — by whom she cannot tell. She assumes it is hers, having arranged the silver sales, and begins saying goodbyes Wren doesn't understand. Beat: dramatic irony tightening like a knot.

chapters.title: Halloway's Ledger
chapters.summary: Halloway's POV. Halloway discovers the margins have been copied and understands Wren has read them. Rather than seize the boy, he offers him a bargain: deliver the original margins and the Eastwicks' father's old debt — the true source of their ruin — will be forgiven. Beat: corruption offering absolution at interest.

chapters.title: The Father's Debt
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren decodes the entry about his own father: the debt that broke the family was manufactured by Halloway to buy Marsh's silence, and Marsh refused, costing the boatman his life and the Eastwicks their name. Wren's survival these three years was itself part of the payment. Beat: the personal cost of other men's power made explicit.

chapters.title: Confrontation at the Chapel
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren brings the atlas to the dying Marsh, who asks forgiveness he does not ask cleanly — he asks Wren to finish the erasure, burning the confession pages so Halloway can never use them. Wren sees the master whole for the first time: brilliant, cowardly, loving. Beat: disillusionment without hatred.

chapters.title: Voss Turns
chapters.summary: Voss's POV. Voss, shadowing Wren, learns Marsh lives and decides the berth and the confession both belong to him — he has suffered longest. He alerts Halloway to the chapel in exchange for his own pardon, betraying everyone at once. Beat: survival's logic devouring loyalty.

chapters.title: The Raid
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs interleaved. Halloway's men raid the chapel; Fen dies holding the door; Marsh gives Wren the confession pages and the berth papers and stays behind to burn the chapel archive himself. Wren escapes with Bette through the marsh channels he mapped but never walked. Beat: the map becomes the territory.

chapters.title: One Berth
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. On the shingle at dawn, with the Kestrel's boat waiting and Halloway's riders close, Wren must choose. Bette forces the choice by revealing she sold the silver to pay for two berths — and the second was always meant for him. He puts her aboard with the atlas as her credential and proof against Halloway. Beat: sacrifice chosen freely at last.

chapters.title: The Burning Page
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Cornered, Wren bargains with Halloway using the one thing left: he reads aloud the page naming Halloway's own payments, then feeds it to the fire piece by piece as Halloway watches, destroying the proof and the threat together. Halloway lets him live because a dead apprentice invites questions. Beat: power meeting its own reflection.

chapters.title: Ash and Ink
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. The workshop is searched and stripped; the atlas is gone to sea inside Bette's trunk. Wren takes up his master's pens and begins a new chart — not of coasts but of the marsh paths, the chapel, the debts — a private atlas of what actually happened. Beat: memory refusing erasure.

chapters.title: Letters Returned
chapters.summary: Alternating letters, Bette's and Wren's POVs. From a port town abroad, Bette uses the atlas to win work with a merchant house; her letters carry the master's cipher in the margins, a language only Wren can read. The last letter says simply: the berth was yours all along, and you gave it well. Beat: grief transmuted into inheritance.

chapters.title: A Bridge for the Letter
chapters.summary: Wren's POV, years later. An aging Wren, now a maker of charts for ordinary people, receives a final letter in the master's hand — written by Bette, who learned the script, carrying news that Marsh died forgiven and unnamed. Wren adds one bridge to his marsh atlas where none existed, and walks it. Beat: the price of survival acknowledged, and paid forward.
